newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU back on track ahead of EU's Amsterdam summit.
newsitem.headline: EMU back on track ahead of EU's Amsterdam summit.

text.p: Europe's single currency project appeared to be back on track ahead of a European Union summit next week after a compromise has emerged over the new French government's reluctance to back a vital pact on strict borrowing limits.

A flurry of diplomatic activity over the past few days has allayed fears that France might scuttle the timetable for the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) by reopening talks on the budget stability pact, a measure designed to keep spending under control among participants of the single currency.

But after France's European partners rushed to show they shared Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's concern for the social aspects of the union, Paris appeared be content to have its focus on employment addressed through two political declarations that will accompany the budget accord.

EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy on Friday said the additions to the pact would be "a sort of economic pillar at the heart of economic and monetary union to allow member states to conduct economic policy in a much more co-ordinated, close and concerted way."

One resolution will focus on jobs creation while the other will address economic policy co-ordination among EMU members. Both are seen amplifying what is already included in the Maastricht Treaty and given their non-binding nature should be easily approved.

In addition, the Amsterdam summit will agree on a separate employment chapter, a revision to the treaty long desired by a number of countries but resisted by Germany because of the potential for expensive jobs programmes.

In a good-will gesture towards the French, Bonn dropped its opposition after getting assurances that the amendment would make no mention of additional spending plans and refer instead to the need for greater EU co-ordination and co-operation in promoting jobs.
The concessions to France on employment should allow EU leaders to ratify the stability and growth pact and re-inject much needed political momentum to the single currency.
They also boost chances that the euro, as the new currency is due to be called, will include a large number of members from its start in 1999, implying a weaker than originally expected currency.

Avinash Persuad, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan in London, says financial markets have concluded a "softened path" for EMU, the consequence of which will be downward pressure on the German mark.
Evidence of such thinking has been seen in recent days with the mark shedding some of the gains made against the dollar and other European currencies earlier in the week.

Whether the soft euro scenario will extend as far as Rome is still unclear, but speaking on German television, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer on Thursday said he was not opposed to Italy joining EMU. "Every country has the same chance (to join EMU)," he said. "Italy has the same chance as every other country."

Germany, long committed to a strict interpretation to the entry criteria for the euro, is under pressure to allow a more flexible approach since it is also facing problems meeting the targets, especially the key one limiting the budget deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
And Thursday's economic forecasts by the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), rich nations' think-tank, seemed to put Germany, France and Italy on equal footing.

The Paris-based organisation forecast all three would show a total public deficit of 3.2 percent of GDP in 1997, and its chief economist Stephen Potter indicated the institution was in favour of a broad euro start.
"The decision will be political," he told a news conference. "From an economic point of view, it would seem anomalous to exclude a few countries on the basis of a few decimal points."
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Thursday he would not be drawn into a debate over how much latitude governments would have in meeting the deficit target.
"I will not engage in a discussion about decimal points," Waigel told German television. "If Germany were to discuss figures like 3.3 or 3.2 percent, others would start to talk about 3.8 percent."

Yet Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg, who is expected to become the head of European central bank once euro starts, said in a newspaper interview that a deficit of 3.2 percent would not be a disaster for the stability of the currency.
